input.heading: Today we are learning to

content.text: Calculate the mean rate of reaction in cm³/s from gas volume and measured time.
Describe how to investigate the effect of hydrochloric acid concentration on its reaction with magnesium, measuring gas volume over time and controlling the mass of magnesium and temperature.
Explain why increasing hydrochloric acid concentration increases the rate of reaction with magnesium, using collision theory and the frequency of successful collisions.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 3 minutes tracing the gas path from flask to syringe. Ask pupils to identify what is measured and how the measurement could be used to calculate a rate.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think the gas syringe measures the acid or the magnesium. It measures the volume of hydrogen gas collected. They may also treat the rate as the final gas volume alone; rate includes time taken.

Background
The reaction is magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. The hydrogen pushes the syringe plunger outwards, so its volume can be read directly.

content.text: Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas and magnesium chloride.
A gas syringe collects hydrogen so its volume can be measured.
Mean rate is the gas volume produced divided by the time taken.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes modelling the calculation. Have pupils copy the three steps, then check that they can explain why the answer has units of cm³/s.

Answers
1. Mean rate = gas volume ÷ time
2. Mean rate = 48 cm³ ÷ 24 s
3. Mean rate = 2 cm³/s

Misconceptions
Pupils may multiply 48 by 24, or give 2 cm³ without a time unit. Rate is volume divided by time, so the unit is cm³/s.

Background
A mean rate gives the average volume produced per second across the measured time. It does not say that gas was produced at exactly the same rate every second.

Running
Allow about 3 minutes for pupils to answer independently, then ask them to show the division they used and explain their choice.

Answers
C: B

Misconceptions
A, 30 cm³/s, suggests pupils multiplied 60 by 30. C, 2 cm³/s, suggests they may have remembered the previous example or divided incorrectly. Calculate 60 ÷ 30 = 2 cm³/s.

Background
The volume and time must use compatible units; here the volume is in cm³ and the time is in seconds, so the rate is in cm³/s.

content.text: What is the mean rate when 60 cm³ forms in 30 seconds?

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 7 minutes. Pupils work in pairs to identify the changed variable, the measured outcome and the controls. Ask them to put the procedure into a clear sequence and explain why readings are taken at regular intervals.

Misconceptions
Pupils may change magnesium mass, acid volume or temperature as well as concentration, making it unclear what caused a rate difference. Keep those variables the same and change only acid concentration. They may also forget that the bung must be fitted promptly, allowing hydrogen to escape and making the measured volume unreliable.

Background
A fair test changes one independent variable—in this investigation, acid concentration—and measures the dependent variable, the gas volume over time. Repeats help identify anomalous results and improve reliability.

content.text: Add a measured volume of hydrochloric acid to a flask; connect it to a gas syringe.
Add a measured mass of magnesium, quickly fit the bung and start the timer.
Record the gas volume at regular time intervals until it stops increasing; repeat for reliability.
Repeat with different acid concentrations, keeping acid volume, magnesium mass and temperature the same; compare mean rates.

input.heading: Why does concentrated acid react faster?

reasons.head: More particles
reasons.line: Higher concentration means more acid particles in the same volume.

reasons.head: More collisions
reasons.line: Acid particles collide with the magnesium surface more frequently.

reasons.head: Faster reaction
reasons.line: Successful collisions happen more frequently, so hydrogen is produced more quickly.

content.text: Why does concentrated acid react faster?
Higher concentration means more acid particles in the same volume.
Acid particles collide with the magnesium surface more frequently.
Successful collisions happen more frequently, so hydrogen is produced more quickly.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes discussing the particle model. Ask pupils to link the number of acid particles per volume to collision frequency, then to the rate of reaction.

Misconceptions
Pupils may say that higher concentration makes each acid particle move faster, or that particles themselves become more reactive. It means there are more acid particles in each unit of volume, so collisions with magnesium happen more frequently. Only successful collisions lead to reaction.

Background
Collision theory explains reaction rate in terms of particles colliding. For this reaction, a successful collision between acid particles and the magnesium surface results in reaction; a greater frequency of successful collisions increases the rate.

elements.alt: A higher concentration has more acid particles in the same volume and more frequent successful collisions with magnesium.

content.text: More acid particles per volume cause more frequent collisions with magnesium.

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 8 minutes. Pupils answer all three tasks independently, then compare their working in pairs. Review the calculation and the controlled variables as a class.

Answers
1. 3 cm³/s
2. Use the same volume of hydrochloric acid, mass of magnesium and temperature each time. Change only the acid concentration. Measure hydrogen volume at regular time intervals with a gas syringe, then compare mean rates. Repeat for reliability.
3. No. 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4 cm³/s, which exceeds 2 cm³/s.

Misconceptions
For the first task, pupils may multiply 84 by 28; divide volume by time to get 3 cm³/s. For the fair comparison, changing magnesium mass, acid volume or temperature as well as concentration would make the result hard to interpret; keep these fixed. For the final task, pupils may compare 72 with 2 without using the time; calculate 72 ÷ 30 = 2.4 cm³/s.

Background
The comparison asks pupils to combine a rate calculation with the fair-test method. A higher mean rate is a larger volume of gas produced per second.

content.text: A reaction produces 84 cm³ of hydrogen in 28 seconds. Calculate its mean rate.
How would you compare two acid concentrations fairly when magnesium reacts with the acid?
A reaction produces 72 cm³ in 30 seconds. Would its mean rate exceed 2 cm³/s?

question.modelAnswer:
1. 3 cm³/s
2. Use the same acid volume, magnesium mass and temperature; record gas volume over time for each concentration.
3. Yes, 2.4 cm³/s

slides.notes:
Running
Allow about 8 minutes for pupils to complete the exit ticket independently. Collect or review responses to identify who can calculate with units, name the controls and connect concentration to successful collision frequency.

Answers
1. 3 cm³/s
2. Change only the hydrochloric acid concentration. Use the same acid volume, magnesium mass and temperature for each test. Add the magnesium, fit the bung promptly and start the timer. Measure gas volume with a gas syringe at regular intervals until it stops increasing; repeat and compare mean rates.
3. Increasing concentration means more acid particles per unit volume. They collide with the magnesium more frequently, so there are more successful collisions each second and the reaction is faster.

Misconceptions
Pupils may give 45 ÷ 15 with no unit; the rate is 3 cm³/s. In the investigation answer, changing more than concentration makes it an unfair test; keep acid volume, magnesium mass and temperature constant. In the explanation, ‘more particles’ alone is incomplete unless linked to more frequent successful collisions with magnesium.

Background
The exit ticket brings together all three lesson objectives: calculating mean rate, planning a fair investigation and explaining the rate change using collision theory.

content.text: A reaction produces 45 cm³ of gas in 15 seconds. Calculate its mean rate.
How would you investigate acid concentration's effect on magnesium, measuring gas and controlling variables?
Why does increasing acid concentration increase the rate of its reaction with magnesium?

question.modelAnswer:
1. 3 cm³/s
2. Measure gas volume over time at different concentrations, keeping magnesium mass, acid volume and temperature the same.
3. More acid particles per volume cause more frequent successful collisions with magnesium, increasing the reaction rate.
